A1.justification: Both PDFs describe DC-Gen and provide readable methods, equations, figures, tables, and appendices sufficient for reliable comparison. v3 substantially extends the same research work.

before.justification: v1 reports original ImageNet class-to-image experiments, SANA and FLUX evaluations, component ablations, and inference benchmarks.

after.justification: v3 reports original image generation, video generation, image editing, human evaluation, and video-autoencoder experiments, including extensive appendix results.

M1.justification: The core embedding-alignment and LoRA pipeline is retained, but v3 introduces DC-AE-V with chunk-causal temporal modeling and a video encoder, decoder, and discriminator (Section 3.5; Appendix H). It also adapts image-to-video conditioning by repeating the input image four times before encoding. Separately naming patch and output alignment does not itself introduce a new stage: both operations existed in v1.

E1.justification: v3 removes ImageNet class-to-image coverage and adds text-to-video and image-to-video evaluation on VBench/VBench-I2V, bilingual image editing on GEdit, and video reconstruction on Panda70m/UCF101. It adds Aesthetic-4K evaluation and reports training with Pexels/Unsplash images, FusionX-generated videos, and Pico-Banana editing pairs. These substantially change the represented data and task requirements.

E2.justification: The MJHQ comparison removes SANA-1.6B/4.8B and adds Z-Image-Turbo while retaining the other image baselines. New comparisons include Diffusion-4K, video generators, FLUX.1-Kontext, Step1X-Edit, and video autoencoders. Appendices B and G additionally evaluate layer-wise learning-rate decay, gradual LoRA, autoencoder latent alignment, TaylorSeer, and AnyFlow; SVDQuant was already evaluated in v1.

E3.justification: v1 benchmarks latency and throughput with torch.compile; v3 specifies TensorRT and transformer-backbone latency. The reported FLUX output-alignment and end-to-end batch sizes change from 256 to 512 (v1 Table 5; v3 Table 12). New evaluation designs include matched-data fine-tuned controls, fixed-resolution video comparisons, Qwen2.5-based editing assessment, and multi-rater human studies. These are reported protocol changes, not evidence that every retained experiment was rerun.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's combined alignment, LoRA, and guidance-objective ablations, v3 separates patch-embedder and output-layer alignment, tests alternative stabilization and latent-alignment strategies, and extends convergence analyses to video and editing. Appendix H adds chunk-size sensitivity, long-video reconstruction checks, and controlled autoencoder substitutions. Appendix G expands acceleration-combination analyses. The earlier DiT/SANA ablations are removed.

E5.justification: Neither version reports training-seed counts, repeated-run variability, confidence intervals, or significance tests. v3's human studies disclose sample and rater counts and preference percentages, but introduce no uncertainty estimates; those additions concern evaluation design and results.

E6.justification: Retained DC-Gen-FLUX entries change: 1K CLIP Score is 27.94 in v1 Table 2 versus 28.02 in v3 Table 1, while GenEval changes from 0.72 to 0.71. Training and timing settings also change, preventing a controlled performance-gain interpretation. v3 adds substantial video, editing, human-preference, reconstruction, and acceleration results, while removing ImageNet, SANA, and NVIDIA 5090 result sets. Several retained ablation values also change.

T1.justification: Appendix H adds a formal chunk-causal convolution construction and defines total video compression as 3f²t/c (Equation 11), extending the earlier spatial formulation. The main alignment loss and guidance-correction derivation remain substantively equivalent, with expanded algebra in Appendix A. No new theorem or proof is introduced.

C1.justification: v1 centers its contribution on text-to-image acceleration demonstrated with SANA and FLUX. v3 broadens the central applicability claim to image generation, text-to-video, image-to-video, and image editing, and explicitly claims the first effective post-training solution for deeply compressed latent adaptation. The earlier abstract's 138× NVIDIA 5090 claim is removed.

C2.justification: v3 distinguishes failure modes across models, including blurred FLUX outputs, ineffective Qwen edits that copy inputs, and Wan training collapse. Appendix B assigns different roles to patch alignment and output alignment: capability recovery versus faster convergence. Appendix H adds substantive explanations of reconstruction-versus-long-video-generalization tradeoffs and the chunk-size choice, extending v1's more general representation-gap explanation.

D1.justification: v3 substantially expands reproducibility information with model-specific hyperparameters, resolution-lifting schedules, data sources and counts, LoRA settings, stage-wise training costs, decoding-cost breakdowns, and DC-AE-V architecture and padding pseudocode (Appendices E–H). These include newly documented details rather than necessarily changed procedures. Conversely, v1's DiT/SANA settings and explicit project-code link are omitted.

R1.justification: v3 substantially expands positioning around video diffusion, editing, video autoencoders, sparsity, and acceleration. Section 3.4 explicitly contrasts DC-Gen with OpenSora-2.0's latent adaptation, while Appendix H distinguishes chunk-causal modeling from IV-VAE, LTX Video VAE, and Video DC-AE. This goes beyond citation renumbering or bibliographic updates.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, method exposition, and conclusion are extensively rewritten. Experiments are reorganized by task; the guidance-correction derivation moves into Appendix A; and the former compact appendix becomes separate sections for ablations, visualization, human evaluation, settings, costs, acceleration combinations, and the video autoencoder. The narrative changes substantially alongside the scientific expansion.

P2.justification: v3 replaces the opening image-only showcase with a multi-task figure and redraws the pipeline to display patch alignment, output alignment, and fine-tuning separately. It adds training curves, human-study tables and interfaces, video/editing comparisons, and autoencoder diagrams. Existing cost and ablation displays are relocated or reorganized, and the main image table replaces throughput with latency.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens support for the central alignment and quality-preservation claims. Unlike v1's bundled alignment ablation, Appendix B isolates the two alignment components and tests credible alternatives; matched-data controls and human studies improve assessment of retained capabilities. Expanded implementation and cost documentation also improves auditability. These gains outweigh the lost ImageNet/SANA coverage and code-link disclosure. Reporting weaknesses remain: Figure 22 gives a 14.8× video speedup at 2160p, whereas Table 16 implies about 9.2×, and statistical uncertainty remains unreported.
